questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given in Polar Coordinates
questions.problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $(6,{45}^{∘}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate od $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ x & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡({45}^{∘}) \\ x & =6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ x & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ y & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡({45}^{∘}) \\ y & =6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ y & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(3\sqrt{2},3\sqrt{2}).$

questions.problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{\pi }{4})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(\frac{r}{2},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$  Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(3\sqrt{2},3\sqrt{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3\sqrt{2})^{2}+(3\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18+18} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(\frac{6}{2},\frac{5\pi }{6})=(3,\frac{5\pi }{6}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =3(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =3(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{3}{2}).$

questions.problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(\sqrt{2},\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(8,\theta +\pi ).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-1}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the third quadrant, we have $\theta =\pi +{\theta }_{R}=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(8,\frac{5\pi }{4}+\pi )=(8,\frac{9\pi }{4})=(8,\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =8\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =8\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(4\sqrt{2},4\sqrt{2}).$

$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(4,\frac{5\pi }{6}),$ we must have $r=4.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $4,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $4.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{5\pi }{6},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\frac{5\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(4,\frac{2\pi }{3})$ 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =4\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-2,2\sqrt{3}).$

Notice that one must traverse the circle clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is ${240}^{∘},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}={240}^{∘}-{210}^{∘}={30}^{∘}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(4,{30}^{∘})$ 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡({30}^{∘}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡({30}^{∘}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(2\sqrt{3},2).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given in Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $\left( 6,\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x &= r\cos\theta\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\[5pt]
		 &= 3
	}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		y &= r\sin\theta\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\[5pt]
		 &= 3\sqrt{3}
	}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $\left(3, 3\sqrt{3}\right).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given a Description of the Radius and Angle
canonical_examples.problem: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $2,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of $135^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ where

$$
r=2, \quad \theta=135^{\circ}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x &= r\cos\theta\[5pt]
		 &=2 \cos\left( 135^{\circ} \right)\[5pt]
		 &= 2 \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
		 &= -\sqrt{2}
	}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		y &= r\sin\theta\[5pt]
		 &= 2 \sin\left(135^{\circ}\right)\[5pt]
		 &= 2 \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
		 &= \sqrt{2}
	}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $\left(  -\sqrt{2},  \sqrt{2}\right).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given Some Information About Another Point
canonical_examples.problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $\left(r, \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \right)$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $\left(5r,\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(3,-\sqrt{3}).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\eqalign{
		r &= \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\[3pt]
		 &=\sqrt{3^2+(\sqrt{3})^2}\[3pt]
		 &= \sqrt{12} \[3pt]
		 &= 2\sqrt{3}
	}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
\left(5(2\sqrt{3}),\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\left(10\sqrt{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x &= r\cos\theta\[5pt]
		&=10\sqrt{3} \cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \right)\[5pt]
		&= 10\sqrt{3} \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\[5pt]
		&= -15
	}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		y &= r\sin\theta\[5pt]
		&=10\sqrt{3} \sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \right)\[5pt]
		&= 10\sqrt{3} \cdot\dfrac{1}{2} \[5pt]
		&=5\sqrt{3}
	}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $\left( -15,  5\sqrt{3}\right).$

canonical_examples.problem:
The diagram below shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $\left(3,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and $m \angle AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952748/assets/a0d06318ba26eee754bc3581f5a0f1c126eb0723f8aea2cac0fad075ee56e7f9.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $\left(3,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right),$ we must have $r=3.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $3,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $3.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle counterclockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ the $\theta$-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
\theta_B = \dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $\left(3,\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x &= r\cos\theta\[5pt]
		 &=3\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \right)\[5pt]
		 &=3\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
		 &=-\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2}
	}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		y &= r\sin\theta\[5pt]
		 &= 3\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \right)\[5pt]
		 &= 3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\[5pt]
		 &=\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2}
	}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $\left(-\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2}\right).$
